judge.notes: The front page clearly delivers a card grid: each story is a bordered, shadowed box with a bold title, a domain pill, and metadata along the bottom, and it drops to one column at 375px as briefed. The thread page uses nested cards with a left indent for replies, which matches the brief's comment structure. Missing pieces: the cards show a top accent border and no visible article/heading hierarchy cue beyond bold text, and the 1280px grid leaves the 4th column of short cards and the bottom row unevenly filled. Metadata wraps awkwardly (e.g. 'ago | 1 comments' breaks across lines), and the 'More' button and footer are fine but the bottom of the page is empty space.

The front page delivers a clear vertical spine with age labels as the most prominent metadata and titles branching off each node, matching the brief's grammar closely. The thread page uses nested spines with comment nodes and indentation, which reads well. At 375px the spine and timestamps still hold up and titles stay dominant, though the 1280px front page leaves a wide empty gutter on the left and the metadata lines are small. The <time> requirement appears satisfied visually through the age labels.

The front page delivers a clear card grid: four across at 1280px, single column at 375px, each story a bordered card with a bold title, a domain pill tag, and a metadata row along the bottom. Comments on the thread page are nested cards with visible left indents and colored rules, matching the brief. Gaps: the metadata wraps awkwardly (e.g. 'comments' orphaned on its own line) and the card titles are not visibly distinguished as h2/h3 in the rendering, and the thread card's top accent differs from the grid cards without clear reason.

The front page realizes the vertical timeline well: a continuous spine with orange dots, ages large and right-aligned on the left, and titles branching right, so the brief is recognizable at a glance. The thread page shows the story as a spine node, but comments are rendered as indented quoted blocks with left rules rather than clearly nested spine nodes, so the comment-timeline part of the brief is only partly met. At 375px the ages wrap awkwardly into narrow columns (e.g. '1 hour ago' split over three lines), and the metadata lines wrap heavily, though nothing overflows. Ages are visibly the most prominent metadata, as requested.

The front page reads as a true spreadsheet: a bordered table with uppercase column headers for title, domain, score, author, age and comments, right-aligned numerals, and a single yellow highlight on the lead row, which matches the brief closely. Weaknesses: the font is proportional rather than monospace or tabular-figure throughout, and the narrow columns at 375px wrap titles into one-word-per-line ribbons, so the mobile view is hard to scan. The frozen header and thin grid are only partly realized, and the thread page is not in table form, so the spreadsheet grammar does not carry over to it.

The candidate reads convincingly as a dense monospace terminal: one story per line, a numbered gutter, prompt-like parentheses, and a single face throughout, with a dark palette and nested thread indentation. However, the fields are not in fixed columns, since points, author, and age float with the title length, and the 375px view wraps each story across four or more lines. The title is bold and the metadata is dimmed, so hierarchy holds, but the prompt markers are minimal and the code-element requirement is only partly evident in the rendered output.

The front page reads as index cards: bordered cards in a three-column grid with uppercase sans labels (POINTS, BY, AGE, DOMAIN, COMMENTS), typewriter values, and red rubber-stamp points badges, so the brief is recognizable at a glance. The metadata is visually a label/value grid, but the brief's required dt/dd structure is not evident from the render and cannot be verified. The 375px view stacks cards cleanly, though the thread page drops the card treatment for plain bordered comment blocks, and the palette shifts toward a bright cream rather than a clearly manila-and-ink institutional tone. Cards are dense and scannable, though the title type is small relative to the card area.

The candidate closely follows the warm paper brief: cream ground, dark brown ink, a serif title face, small-caps metadata running under each title, and a book-measure column with no gutter numbering. The front page reads as prose entries rather than cards, a genuinely different shape from the live site. The thread page nests comments with left rules and indentation, which makes depth visible, though the text is somewhat dense. I cannot verify from screenshots that each story is an article element or that no ol/ul sits in main, and the brief's broadside character is only partly realized, since the page feels more like a clean book page than a bold printed sheet.

The front page delivers a genuine card grid: four across at 1280px, one column at 375px, with titles as bold headings, domain tags as small pills, and metadata along the bottom of each card, which matches the brief closely. The thread page nests comments as bordered cards with visible left indents, as requested. Titles are clearly dominant and the mint domain tags are restrained, though some cards have uneven heights leaving gaps under short titles, and the 375px view uses a single long column with the card metadata wrapping awkwardly. The header nav pills are a nice touch but the brief's structural requirements of article/h2 elements cannot be confirmed visually.

The front page delivers a clear vertical spine with dot nodes, and ages sit on the left of the spine as the most prominent metadata in green, matching the brief's emphasis. Titles branch off the spine with metadata beneath, and the thread page uses nested spines with smaller nodes for comments, as requested. The 375px view keeps the spine and age column intact without overflow, though long titles wrap heavily in the narrow column. The brief's requirement that each age be a time element cannot be verified from screenshots, and the thread page's nested depth is only lightly differentiated by indentation.

The front page reads clearly as index cards: manila fill, ink borders, red top rule, a stamp-like circle, and every card shows labelled uppercase sans fields (POINTS, BY, AGE, DOMAIN, COMMENTS) with typewriter values, and the metadata appears to be a dl structure. The palette is muted with one rubber-stamp red as the brief asked. Weaknesses: the grid's ragged card heights leave empty space in shorter cards, the thread page drops the card grammar for the nested comment view and only uses the card for the story header, and the 375px view stacks cards cleanly but makes the list long. The grid also lacks the fixed-width index-card feel at the 1280px width of the cards' content.

The front page reads as a long-form column with no list bullets, no rules, no borders, and no gutter numbers, and the warm neutral palette and serif headlines match the brief's quiet direction. Metadata sits quietly under each title and the 375px version reflows cleanly. The brief asked for each story to be a short prose block in a single comfortable measure, but the stories are only lightly prose-like, with the title and byline reading as a standard stacked list. The thread page is nicely nested with indentation, though the comment hierarchy is shallow and the sans-serif metadata against serif body text is a little uneven.

The front page follows the cards-on-a-grid brief closely: bordered rounded cards with bold titles, domain pill tags, and metadata along the bottom, arranged 4-across at 1280px and single column at 375px. The thread page nests comments as indented cards with left rules, matching the brief. Cards have uneven heights, leaving some dead space above the metadata divider, and the 375px view stacks cleanly without overflow. The brief's requirement for the title to be an h2 or h3 is plausibly met, though the metadata line wraps awkwardly on several cards.

The front page clearly delivers a vertical spine with timestamp nodes and titles branching right, with age as the most prominent metadata in teal, which matches the brief well. The thread page is weak: it shows only one deleted comment node and a nearly empty canvas, so the nested comment spine is barely demonstrated. At 375px the timeline holds together without overflow, though the spine is cramped and the header nav wraps awkwardly.

The front page is a genuine table with visible Title, Domain, Score, Author, Age and Comments headers, thin cell grid, monospace figures and right-aligned numbers, and a single yellow highlight on the lead row, so the spreadsheet brief reads at a glance. However, the brief's frozen header feel is not evident and the Title column is oversized while Domain and Author wrap awkwardly into narrow cells. At 375px the table overflows horizontally, clipping the Comments column and squeezing titles into one-word-per-line columns, which is hard to scan. The thread page keeps the table header for the story and uses indented prose for comments, which is a reasonable adaptation.

The candidate reads clearly as a library card catalog: manila cards, ink top rules, typewriter values, and rubber-stamp red domain tags, with a card grid that is a genuinely different page shape from the live table. However, the uppercase sans labels are present but the brief's labelled fields are only partly carried through, and the thread page drops the card treatment for plain nested blocks, so the catalog metaphor weakens there. At 375px the cards stack cleanly with no overflow, though the three-column grid leaves the 1280px view dense with small type and the lower cards are cut off in the screenshot.

The front page is a genuine data grid with a thin-celled table, visible TITLE/DOMAIN/POINTS/BY/AGE/COMMENTS headers, right-aligned numerics in monospace, and a single highlighted lead row, so the brief is clearly realized. Novelty is high because the shape is a table rather than the live stacked cards. Craft suffers at 375px: the DOMAIN and BY columns collapse into one-letter-per-line vertical strips, making rows enormously tall and the page nearly unscannable, and the frozen header feel is not evident. The 1280px thread page reuses the table only for the story header and the comments remain prose blocks, which is reasonable but the nesting is shown mainly by indentation. The 'frozen header' and tabular rank column are absent.

The candidate reads immediately as a library catalog: manila background, ink text, index-card boxes with double top rules, uppercase sans labels, typewriter values, and a single rubber-stamp red THREAD mark, all matching the brief. Its vertical single-column card stack is a genuinely different shape from the live four-column grid. Craft is decent at 375px with no overflow, but the cards are long and repetitive with a lot of vertical scroll, the thread page leaves a large empty area, and the brief's requirement of a dl per story is plausibly met but the value column is wide and sparse; the 'comments' label is visible but cards lack a distinct card-title hierarchy beyond underlined serif titles.

The front page follows the brief closely: every story is a bordered, shadowed card with a heading, a domain pill, and metadata along the bottom, arranged in a 4-across grid at 1280px that collapses to one column at 375px. Cards have colored top borders and the layout reads clearly as a card grid, a genuinely different shape from the timeline list. Weaknesses: the metadata wraps awkwardly ('| 125 / comments' splits across lines), many cards have large empty lower areas, and the thread page's nested comments use thin left rules rather than clearly distinct nested cards, so the required card-nesting is only partly realized.

The front page delivers a clear vertical spine with age as the most prominent metadata, right-aligned in bold italic rust color, and each title branching off a dot node, matching the brief's grammar. The thread page uses nested spines with comment nodes, though the spine lines and indentation get faint and the nesting depth is only weakly differentiated. At 375px the timeline holds up with the age column and titles readable, but titles wrap heavily and the metadata lines break awkwardly. Overall it reads as a genuinely different page shape from the live site's boxed list.

The brutalist brief is clearly realized: heavy black bordered article blocks, huge rank numerals, no rounded corners, and system sans-serif type with metadata in plain black. Thick rules sit between stories, satisfying the hr requirement visually, though the 1280px page shows the numbers and blocks well while the 375px view stacks cleanly with only minor wrapping of metadata. The thread page has nested bordered comment blocks with a thick left rule for depth, but the bottom footer block is small and the lower half of the page is largely empty, and the numbers are not as huge as the brief suggests.

The front page reads clearly as a vertical timeline: a continuous spine with dot nodes, ages right-aligned in bold red as the most prominent metadata, and titles branching off the spine. The thread page uses nested spines with indented comment nodes, matching the brief. Gaps: the front page at 375px is a long single column with the age labels wrapping awkwardly (e.g. '3 HOURS AGO' split over three lines), and the age text isn't clearly visible as <time> from the screenshot. Titles are set in a heavy serif with underlines, so the hierarchy is clear but the metadata lines are fairly quiet.

The front page reads as index cards: manila fill, dark top rule, rubber-stamp red circle, uppercase sans labels with typewriter values, and a card grid that differs strongly from the live timeline. The brief's dl/dt/dd structure is plausibly implemented since labels sit beside values, though labels are small and light, and the palette leans slightly yellow rather than muted institutional. At 375px cards stack cleanly with no overflow. The thread page keeps the card for the story header but comments are plain bordered boxes with weak differentiation between nesting levels and a serif body that reads somewhat dense.

The front page reads clearly as a vertical timeline: a continuous spine with orange node markers, ages right-aligned on the spine and titles branching off it, and the age is the most saturated metadata. The thread page uses nested spines for comments as the brief asked. Craft is held back at 375px where the ages and titles wrap heavily and the spine sits tight against text, and on the front page the metadata lines are small and the title-to-meta gap is tight. The brief's required <time> elements cannot be verified from screenshots, and the thread page leaves a large empty area below the footer.

The front page clearly delivers the brutalist brief: heavy black bordered blocks with hard offset shadows, huge point numbers, system sans fonts, no rounded corners, and a black header with boxed nav. The brief asked for metadata in plain black, which is met, but the numbers and titles compete for attention and the stories are very tall, so only about ten fit per screen. The 375px view reflows cleanly, though titles wrap heavily. The thread page is sparse, with one story and one comment, and the <hr> separators between stories were not verified as present at the required count from the screenshots alone.

The front page reads as a true vertical timeline: a spine with orange node circles, ages set as the most prominent metadata on the left, and titles branching off the spine, with the age element sitting left of each node. The thread page nests comments on a secondary spine with smaller nodes, which matches the brief. Missing pieces: the brief's age-on-spine idea is only partly realized on the thread page where the story age is not prominent, and the 375px front page wraps ages awkwardly ('16 hours / ago') and the age column squeezes titles. The thread page has a large empty area at the bottom and the nested comment nodes are small but legible.

The front page reads clearly as index cards: manila fill, dashed rule under each title, uppercase sans labels (DOMAIN, POINTS, BY, AGE, COMMENTS) with typewriter values, and a single rubber-stamp red DISCUSS button, matching the brief closely. The grid of three cards at 1280px is a genuinely different page shape from the live list, though the card stack at 375px becomes a long single column that makes scanning 30 stories slow. The thread page keeps the red-stamped card header, but the comment nesting is only a thin left rule and the code blocks dominate, so the thread hierarchy is weaker than the front page. Palette is coherent and restrained, with the red reserved for stamps and the header accent.

The front page is a true prose-block reading view: each story is a title, a small domain note, and a metadata line in a single measure, with no list, borders, rules, or gutter numbers, and warm cream neutrals with serif type. Hierarchy relies on size and weight as the brief asks, and the 375px view reflows cleanly with no overflow. The brief's required section/article structure is not visible in the screenshots, and the metadata lines are slightly louder than needed in their orange-brown link color. The thread page nests comments with indentation and keeps comfortable line length, though the deep nesting narrows the text noticeably by the third level.

The front page is a true data grid with a visible th header row, thin cell borders, right-aligned numeric columns for score and comments, and only the lead row highlighted in yellow, which matches the brief closely. At 375px the table keeps all columns but squeezes them, so the age and comments columns are clipped off the right edge and the title column wraps heavily, which hurts scannability. Numbers are not clearly monospace or tabular-figure styled, and the thread page reuses the table header well but leaves a large empty area below the comments.

The pastel soft-card direction is clearly realized: rounded pastel cards with gentle shadows and dark text on the front page, and a soft card header on the thread page. However, the brief asks for pill-shaped tags for domain and comment count, and the comment count and domain do appear as pills, which is good, but the card layout is a single vertical stack rather than a distinctly soft-UI app surface, and avatar-like spacing is not evident. Novelty is limited because the page is still a single-column list of the same story rows as the live site, only restacked and recolored. At 375px the layout reflows cleanly with no overflow, though the metadata wraps awkwardly and the nav pills wrap onto two rows.

The front page follows the pastel soft UI brief well: rounded pastel cards with gentle shadows, dark text, and pill-shaped score and comment tags on a three-column masonry grid. The brief's required structure is only partly visible, since the domain sits in a small monospace tag but the comment count is a pill rather than clearly inside a small element, and the thread page's comment nesting is shown only by indentation. At 375px the cards stack cleanly, though the nav pill wraps awkwardly and some comment pills break onto their own lines. Ranking is weaker than it could be because the cards have very uneven heights and large empty bottom areas.

The front page has a clear hierarchy: a large lead story, bold serif titles, then small-caps metadata, and a tidy two-column grid with consistent rules between entries. The palette is restrained cream with dark green and rust accents, which feels intentional and still reads as a news page. The 375px view stacks cleanly but metadata wraps awkwardly (points and comments split onto a second line) and the lead title is heavy. On the thread page, the green left bars and progressive indentation make nesting depth legible, though the nested indents shrink the measure quickly and deep replies look crowded toward the right edge.

brief: newspaper broadsheet: serif masthead, columns, hairline rules, small caps for metadata

judge.notes: The front page at 1280px has a clear title-over-metadata hierarchy with bold serif titles, small-caps metadata, and a restrained cream palette that reads as a news page. The two-column layout keeps 30 stories skimmable, with rank numbers hanging in the margin and a thin vertical rule separating columns. At 375px the single column holds up, though metadata wraps awkwardly (words like 'com-ments' and 'com-' break across lines) and the header nav wraps messily. The thread page uses green left borders and indentation to show nesting, which works, but the italic body text at this size is somewhat tiring to read over long comments.

The front page has a distinct warm-paper, serif editorial look with small-caps metadata that stays quieter than the bold titles, and the two-column 30-story grid at 1280px is easy to skim with numbers aligned in a consistent gutter. The lead story is given appropriate prominence without competing too hard with the rest. The thread page uses nested left rules in green and grey that make comment depth visible, though the deepest replies get squeezed toward the right edge and the italic body text in long comments is a bit tiring to read. Overall it is restrained and coherent, with some hierarchy weakness in the thread view and a large unused area below the footer on the front page.

The front page uses a warm cream background with a serif face, bold titles, and small-caps metadata that stays visibly quieter than titles, giving a distinct newspaper-like point of view. Two columns with a rule divider and numbered entries make 30 stories skimmable at 1280px, though the page ends at about 1300px leaving a large empty area below. At 375px the single column works but metadata wraps awkwardly ('com-ments' breaks, orphaned words), and the nav wraps onto a second line. The thread page has clear nesting via left rules and indentation, but the depth lines are faint and the body text is long-measure at full width, reducing comfort.

The front page is dense and very compact, with monospace type that reads clearly, but the line height is tight and the metadata sits inline with titles so it competes with them; wrapped meta lines break awkwardly (e.g. 'comments' orphaned on the next line). The thread page shows nesting via indented left rules, which makes depth visible, though the comment text is a long undifferentiated column with little spacing between comments. Palette is restrained cream and brown with a single accent, which feels intentional and news-like. The 375px front page reflows acceptably but gets long and cramped, with metadata wrapping into ragged lines.
